newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa pleads for cash at African-American summit.
newsitem.headline: Africa pleads for cash at African-American summit.

text.p: African leaders pleaded for U.S. investments at the emotional opening session of an African-American business summit in the Zimbabwean capital on Wednesday.

Presidents Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe, Abdou Diouf of Senegal and Ketumile Masire of Botswana joined forces with Organisation of African unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim to pledge the continent's seriousness towards democracy and economic reform.

Mugabe, whose government banned public portests on Tuesday to stop war veterans demonstrating for pension payouts, urged black Americans to help Africa achieve rapid economic progress, warning that slow growth would breed further political instability in the world's poorest continent.

"The time is over for the soldier-come-soldier-go system of government," he said to about 1,000 delegates who began meeting in Harare on Tuesday to discuss boosting trade, investment and economic aid from the United States to Africa.
"We are therefore resolute in our determination to see the blossoming of sustainable democratic systems of governance on the continent."

While he devoted much of his speech to Africa's need for tangible economic development, Mugabe won rapturous applause from the audience for his parting words: "You are welcome. You are home. You are with your African family."

Masire, whose country balances its budget and has one of the largest foreign reserves in Africa, urged black Americans to help the continent survive the vast changes being wrought by globalisation and liberalisation of trade tariffs.

But he wanted deals, not pledges, saying: "The coming together of Africans and African-Americans in this summit should now move from platitudes to concrete action. Businesses should leave this conference with meaningful partnerships."
Senegal's Diouf, echoing the urgent need for trade and investment, urged the United States to help industrialise Africa.

"Today, with economic globalisation, new rules in world trade and the appearance of emerging economics, African decision-makers and economic operators as well as the international community are facing more than ever the necessity to help our continent resolve its problems and develop," Diouf added.
Salim said Africa was overcoming old perceptions of it as a "hopeless continent" and was undertaking harsh socio-economic reforms to hold up its end of the bargain.
"African countries are seriously engaged in economic development. There is no doubt that Africa is adjusting itself to play a meaningful role in its own development," he said.
The four-day summit has blended business and the clamour for investment with visionary fervour as African-Americans declare their commitment to Africa as their homeland.

Reverend Leon Sullivan, a Baptist and the driving force behind the summit, prompted delegates to whistling their admiration with his preacher-style address urging ambitious projects to rectify Africa's ills.

"We are on a mission of humanity for a forgotten continent," he declared. "We were taken away (as slaves) and made like scrambled eggs with the thought that we would never get together again. We have returned with strength, skills and with money!"
